I now fully understand it. This is the **Task stream** panel. The hover card (`#taskHover`) shows full per-call detail (model, tokens, tok/s, prompt, etc.) on `mouseover`, but:

- It has `pointer-events: none` — you can't scroll/select inside it.
- It hides on `mouseout` — any mouse movement kills it, so you can't study the prompt or copy the call.

I'll add a **pin/expand** interaction: **click a row to pin** the card open (becomes interactive — scroll & select the prompt, copy the call), with **✕ / Esc / click-outside to close**. Hover still works as a quick peek when nothing is pinned.

Done. The Task-stream hover card in Atelier can now be **pinned open so you can study the actual call** instead of it vanishing on any mouse movement.

**What changed** (all in `dashboard/ui/index.html`):

- **Click a task row → pins the card open.** While pinned it becomes interactive (`pointer-events: auto`) so you can **scroll and select/copy** the prompt and metrics. It's also a bit wider (420px) with a brighter gold border so it's clearly the "locked" state.
- **Frozen while pinned** — hovering other rows no longer swaps or hides it, so it doesn't move or disappear on you.
- **Three ways to close:** the **✕** button (top-right, only appears when pinned), **Esc**, or **click anywhere outside** the card.
- **Plain hover still works** as the quick peek (non-interactive, auto-hides) when nothing is pinned.
- Bumped the prompt display cap from 600 → 4000 chars so the full call is actually there to study (the box scrolls).

Behavior verified end-to-end in a real browser (hover → pin → stays frozen → Esc closes).

_**Agent (2026-08-02 07:26:57Z)**_

Done. The **Inference Latency line chart (last 20 req)** — and the tokens/sec sparkline next to it — now give a **rich data card when you hover a point on the line**, the same card style as the task stream.

**What you get hovering a latency point:** the full per-request detail — model, backend, path, status, duration, and (when the live `ollama_perf` feed is present) TTFT, tok/s, in/out tokens — instead of Chart.js's bare number tooltip. The card resolves to the *exact* point you're over (verified: hovering the 63s spike showed `duration 63.0s` with that request's details).

**How it's built (reusable "as needed" for other charts):**
- A shared `.richcard` CSS class now backs both the task-stream card and chart cards (same look, one source of truth).
- New `richChartTooltip` — a Chart.js `external` tooltip handler. Any chart opts in by setting `chart._pointMeta = [meta,…]` parallel to its data and using `{ enabled:false, external: richChartTooltip }`. It renders through the same `_fmtTaskHover`, so meta objects are the identical shape the task stream uses.
- Both mini-line charts pass fallback labels (`{title, unit, kind}`), so a point with no full meta still shows a clean `value (ms)` / `value (tok/s)` card rather than a raw canvas id.
- `_pointMeta` is kept in lockstep with data across **all** four data sources (log tail, live perf ring, log tok/s, predictor avg) via a `pushRing` helper — so the card never shows detail from a stale point.

**Verified in a real browser:** correct point resolution on the latency line, generic-value fallback, hide-on-leave, and the task card still pins/closes correctly after the CSS refactor.

To reuse on another chart (e.g. the memory line): set its `_pointMeta` where you set its data, and switch its tooltip to `{ enabled:false, external: richChartTooltip }`. Want me to wire that into the memory chart too?

One note: the live TTFT/tok-s fields only populate when the governor's capturing proxy is feeding `/telemetry` — otherwise the card shows what the log tail has (model, path, status, duration), same as the task stream.

_**Agent (2026-08-02 07:55:25Z)**_

Both charts are wired and verified. Here's the summary.

## What I did

**Memory chart now has the rich hover card too.** Hovering any point on the memory line gives a card showing:
- **sampled** (time), **baseline (macOS+apps)**, **LLM load**, **resident (live)**, **level**
- an **"in the baseline"** list of the top 5 processes *as they were at that sample* (snapshotted per-point, so historical points keep their own breakdown)

To make it reusable, I extended the shared card renderer (`_fmtTaskHover`) to accept:
- `rows: [[key, value], …]` — arbitrary labeled rows
- `list: { title, items }` — a text block (used for the top-process breakdown)

So now **all four surfaces share one card** (`.richcard` + `richChartTooltip`): task stream, latency line, tokens/sec sparkline, and memory chart. Any future chart opts in with two lines: set `chart._pointMeta = [...]` where you set its data, and use `{ enabled:false, external: richChartTooltip }` in its tooltip config.

Verified in-browser: the memory card renders all rows + the process list + correct source line.

---

## "Do we always have to close, rebuild, and restart?"

**No — and for what we just did, you never need to rebuild.** Every change was in `dashboard/ui/index.html` (pure HTML/JS/CSS, zero Rust). What you do depends on how you're running it:

| How you're running | To see UI changes |
|---|---|
| **`cargo tauri dev`** (README's "Dev / hot-reload") | Just **reload the window (Cmd+R)** — or it auto-reloads on save. No rebuild. This is the loop you want while iterating on the dashboard. |
| **The built `AtelierDashboard.app`** | Must `cargo tauri build` + relaunch. Tauri **compiles the UI into the binary** at build time (that's why `.app/Contents/Resources` has only `icon.icns`, and the bundle is dated Jul 6). A running built app can't see edits to the source `ui/` files. |
| **Just a browser** (`python3 -m http.server` in `dashboard/ui`, like I used to test) | Reload the tab. Fastest loop for pure layout/JS work — the UI degrades gracefully without Tauri (Tauri IPC calls fail, but the governor HTTP fetches still populate most panels). |

**Only Rust edits** (`src-tauri/*.rs`) force a real rebuild + restart — in dev mode `cargo tauri dev` does that automatically on save.

So: run it with `cargo tauri dev` and these hover-card changes show up on a simple **Cmd+R**. The heavy close/rebuild/restart cycle is only needed when you touch the Rust backend or want to ship a new `.app`.

Want me to launch it with `cargo tauri dev` so you can see all the cards live?
